So having Levia first, you're not going to drink as much. I'm excited for law enforcement and regulators to actually get some of this research, because I think it'll inform people more.

Bryan Fields: Yeah, and I've found that when I have a THC beverage first, I always have less alcohol, versus the other way, where if I have a stiff drink, maybe I have a second one and then the beverage. I wonder why that is — maybe it's the inhibitions thing, like I could do another one and drive like a race car, which again isn't the right idea.

Bryan Fields: What do you say for consumers who've had two drinks and then want to try a THC beverage — would you recommend against it? If it's their first or second time, does that matter? At a Super Bowl party, my buddy had a few drinks and wanted to try one, and I encouraged him not to, because I didn't want him to mask what he was feeling from alcohol with THC. Was that the right approach, or would it have been fine for him to try it there?

Eric Rogers: I think you made the right recommendation, especially for a first-time consumer — you want to know what that impact is on your body. You're used to alcohol, and when you consume alcohol then cannabis, it can just feel like an extension of it versus a different effect, depending on the type of cannabis product — could be more cerebral, or way more body, vastly different experiences. We as adult consumers are used to single-substance psychoactives — caffeine, nicotine, alcohol — cause and effect. There are hundreds of cannabinoids in the cannabis plant, and we're extracting all of them out, giving you a full-spectrum experience. That's a much more dynamic experience than the average consumer is even used to. So especially with a first, second, or third-time experience, you want to understand how it's going to interact with your body, understand your dose, how 5, 2.5, or 10 milligrams affects you. Back to the inhibitions point — if you've had a couple of stiff cocktails and have one and still feel good, you might drink more, and you might not realize it, and that's where you might get into overconsumption on the cannabis side. Mixing high doses of both is not a good time — it can be very disorienting for people who've never experienced those two dynamic substances together.

Kristin Rogers: Yeah, we do not want people to have a bad experience, especially the first time. You definitely made the right call.

Bryan Fields: I'm going to tell my mom — have a THC beverage first, then go to the wine.

Bryan Fields: What about cannabinoids, like with edibles there's the trifecta, mixing different cannabinoids — does that work the same with beverages, or is it different given body chemistry?

Eric Rogers: Yeah, it works the same. We're basically taking that full-spectrum oil and encapsulating it — not to oversimplify, but cannabis doesn't like water, so we create a new molecule, one side loves oil, one side loves water, with a certain particle size so it kicks in quickly and consistently. That's our secret sauce. Whatever those minor cannabinoids are — THC, CBD — those are the keys that unlock your endocannabinoid system to let all those minor cannabinoids flow through and give you that full effect, the entourage effect everyone talks about.

Bryan Fields: As a low-dose consumer myself, I notice very quickly when it's only THC — I feel like the existence of other cannabinoids is so important, it's what nature intended. What does the existence of them make you feel like versus straight THC?

Kristin Rogers: When I have straight THC, I get a little more racy, a bit of that paranoia thing, the stigma people have about cannabis. I definitely don't feel the same as when I have a strain given to me the way nature intended, with the soft landing of other cannabinoids. And what's exciting is we're learning more every day about the cannabinoids surrounding THC and what they do and don't do for you. This is a really fun time because we're learning why that is, why those exist in the plant to begin with. We think that disparity — smoking and traditional THC-only edibles versus full spectrum — is part of why smoking continues to dominate as a behavior, because you're getting the full effect as you're smoking, all those cannabinoids converted in real time. So by taking a full-spectrum approach, how do we create an experience that's most like that, in a healthier way for consumers?

Bryan Fields: How do you communicate all that complexity on a can to a consumer? They're looking at packaging, then milligrams probably next — where's the balance between fair, clean, beautiful packaging that sells well, and communicating those finer details?

Eric Rogers: Part of it is we have a certain regulatory framework we have to work within — how do you translate that to execution? You need directions for use — on a drink, I'm not just going to tell you "open can and drink." We tell you a little story on the side about what to expect, giving you that predictable outcome. Right on the front of the can there's a badge with the effect it's going to be, a color that corresponds to that effect, and it tells you what the anticipated outcomes are going to be — you're going to rest and recharge, feel active and alert, feel social and relaxed. We're trying to help frame for consumers what that experience is going to be, from the flavor profile to the milligram strength, using storytelling, infusing fun and brand personality into the packaging, rather than just "drink can, wait 45 minutes before a second." We say, you'll open this up and within the next 15 to 20 minutes you're going to feel this restful, peaceful feeling, and if you're new to it, go slow, drink half a can — communicating the value proposition through packaging, since that's the billboard in the person's hand.

Kristin Rogers: I'll say it's also extremely important to invest in education for budtenders. They're the first line, and people trust them, especially if they haven't had a cannabis experience before. Helping budtenders understand the difference between products is really fun, because people come from all sorts of different industries and backgrounds. Educational posters in the back rooms, events for budtenders only, to learn about your product — we're the only ones making a full-spectrum drink in Massachusetts, so helping them understand why this might be a good opportunity for a first-time consumer is really important, so we get people to come back.

Bryan Fields: I don't know if I've ever read the side of a can — I've just reached into the fridge, cracked it, started drinking, happy, having a good time. Maybe now I should spend more time reading those cans, because there are probably nuanced details that are critical for understanding.

Kristin Rogers: We do get some high-dose consumers who still buy our beverage because they get the minor cannabinoids and it hits them differently, and they enjoy that. So that education piece and really learning about it is really helpful too.

Bryan Fields: Why do you think everything in the cannabis industry takes three to five times longer than expected?

Eric Rogers: I think because there's only so much in your control. You look at a new market coming online, and typically the regulatory body itself is brand new — they're a startup in themselves, so you're only as good as the weakest startup, and when you have to work within the framework of the government to be a startup within that, it's hard. We were the first drink to launch east of Colorado in a regulated market — since hemp hadn't really come on yet — in 2021, and it was a lot to partner with regulators about what drinks even meant. Everything up until that point was entirely weight-based, with a plus-or-minus 10% rule, so if I had a package of 15 pounds of flower, I could be off by a pound and a half and it's still fine — that's like a six-pack out of a case, and they'd say no, you have to buy that for full price right now. So working with regulators to evolve how they were measuring the industry into more unit-based economics versus all weight-based, because they were even trying to limit the number of units on a metrc tag, since one can is the equivalent of 3.55 one-gram joints. So when I have a case, they'd say wait, you can't have all those. It's working within that framework to demystify it. We're very lucky the CCC worked really well with us in the beginning, because they could see it too — like, oh, vault size, we were originally going to have to fit all our drinks into these tiny cages, and it's a big product, too hard. So little things like that were really helpful, and we're still grateful they were willing to work with us on that.

Bryan Fields: Does alcohol have to deal with any of those?

Eric Rogers: No, absolutely not. But that's part of doing something that's federally illegal but legal in your state, and no one else has done it before — so fail forward in those moments, and try to use the regulatory framework to your benefit. Drinks are big, we don't fit into this model, we also need to ship pallets of these, when in the early days our average order size was 100 cases — that was until they realized how big 100 cases was and their vault couldn't fit that. Our manufacturing floor, you have to go through three or four limited-access points before you even get to it, it's at the center of the facility, with 60 cameras in the building — why doesn't this qualify as a vault, why can't I just store drinks on a pallet? It's working through the common-sense stuff as you contextualize what you're doing. But it all leads to everything taking longer, especially when you're doing something new, because there's only so much inside your control. You have to learn patience if you don't have it.

Bryan Fields: That's a really good answer, even though deep down you're probably really frustrated a lot of the time, because common sense is never really the leading decision-maker in this industry.

Eric Rogers: Yeah, still frustrating, we still get used to it. But I remind myself we get to work in an industry that until recently was completely federally illegal, a Schedule I drug, and that was the cost of doing business in that industry, to be a pioneer, to move the industry forward, to normalize, to destigmatize, to put these products out. That's the cost of it. If anyone asks what the number one skill you need in cannabis is, it's perseverance — just not giving up, not panicking but pivoting, based on the ever-changing regulatory environment. If you panic at every moment, you're frozen, but if you can pivot and move in a new direction and continue to ebb and flow with the framework, you'll continue to survive and, dare I say, thrive.

Bryan Fields: Great quote. Last question — what question do you wish more people asked you?

Kristin Rogers: That's a good question. I think everyone assumes we're all rich, because this is federally illegal and it seemed like there was this big boom. No — very few people have made a lot of money in this industry so far, and I think that would be helpful for people to know, because as we're federally regulating and starting to talk about this, everyone's asking for money. Everyone's asking, could we maybe take one step at a time, back up, and allow us to continue to make some money first so we can invest appropriately in marketing and all the things we should be doing.

Bryan Fields: I can imagine the people asking for those things just don't understand the nuances of how 280E works, and how spinning up in different states, and understanding all these outrageous rules and regulations your team has to abide by in order to play the game — those are non-negotiables, that's what it takes to get started. Kristin, Eric, for our listeners who want to get in touch and learn more, where can they find you?

Eric Rogers: www.drinklevia.com. We're just starting our new website, so by the time this goes out it'll be live. We get all the info requests, so if you want to reach out, it comes right to Kristin and me every time. We can each be reached — I'm eric@levia.buzz and Kristin is kristin@levia.buzz. If there are any questions or collaboration opportunities, we're always open to those.

Bryan Fields: Thanks for taking the time, this was a lot of fun.

Kristin Rogers: Thank you so much, really appreciate it.
summary: This episode features Kristin and Eric Rogers, co-founders of cannabis beverage brand Levia, discussing how effects-based drinks are pulling new, often non-smoking consumers into cannabis. They dig into how dosing, formulation, and packaging must adapt state by state, why beverages offer faster onset and more predictable offset than edibles, the role of hemp beverages in expanding market reach, and the ongoing challenge of educating regulators, budtenders, and consumers about mixing cannabis with alcohol and dosing responsibly. It's a useful listen for anyone curious about how cannabis beverage brands build consistency, navigate regulation, and position themselves as a bridge between alcohol culture and cannabis.
takeaways: Success in cannabis can't be measured by how many states a brand operates in, since each state's regulatory system and consumer behavior differ dramatically.
Levia formulates with minor cannabinoids and adjusts packaging/storytelling state by state to maintain a consistent brand experience despite differing dosing caps and input availability.

Beverages offer faster onset and a shorter, more predictable 'offset' (about 3 hours) than edibles, giving consumers more control by letting them simply stop drinking if they feel the effects coming on.
Beverages act as a 'category opener' for consumers uncomfortable with smoking or edibles, especially younger non-drinkers and older generations wary of past bad experiences.
Hemp beverages, with fewer marketing restrictions, are seen as a way to build broader consumer education and a 'halo effect' for the regulated cannabis beverage market.
Cannabis and alcohol affect the body differently — alcohol lowers inhibitions while cannabis heightens awareness of them — which complicates driving-impairment testing and regulatory comparisons.
Educating regulators, lawmakers, and budtenders is viewed as the brand's own responsibility, including facility tours to demystify manufacturing and dosing consistency.

Cannabis industry timelines are consistently longer than expected because regulatory bodies are themselves new 'startups' that companies must help shape (e.g., moving from weight-based to unit-based regulations).

faq.question: Why is being in many states not necessarily a sign of cannabis brand success?
faq.answer: Because each state has its own insulated regulatory system, dosing caps, and consumer behavior, so a brand could be in 35 states and still make less money than one operating well in a single state.

faq.question: How do cannabis beverages differ from edibles in terms of onset and duration?
faq.answer: Beverages use emulsification technology that bypasses the liver, creating faster onset (versus 45 minutes to 2+ hours for edibles) and a more predictable 'offset,' with effects generally fading within about three hours based on THC's half-life, compared to 10-12 hours for edibles.

faq.question: Why are cannabis beverages considered a good entry point for new or hesitant consumers?
faq.answer: They're socially acceptable and don't require removing yourself from a social setting like smoking does, they offer dosing control similar to alcohol, and they let people 'try one and see how it goes' without commitment to a full edible dose.

faq.question: What is the difference in how alcohol and cannabis affect decision-making and driving risk?
faq.answer: Alcohol lowers inhibitions and impairs judgment, often making people feel falsely confident about driving, while cannabis impairs but tends to make users more aware of their own limitations, which is why heavily intoxicated cannabis users often drive overly cautiously rather than recklessly.

faq.question: Is it safe to mix alcohol and cannabis beverages?
faq.answer: According to Kristin Rogers, a licensed substance abuse counselor, mixing high doses of both is not recommended and can cause disorienting effects like nausea; low doses of both may work for some people, but reactions vary widely by individual.

faq.question: Why do full-spectrum cannabinoid products feel different from THC-only products?
faq.answer: Full-spectrum products include minor cannabinoids beyond THC that create an 'entourage effect,' offering a smoother, more grounded experience (less racy or paranoid) compared to isolated THC, which some describe as a 'soft landing' similar to consuming the plant as nature intended.

faq.question: Why does everything in the cannabis industry seem to take three to five times longer than expected?
faq.answer: Because regulatory bodies overseeing legal cannabis are themselves new and evolving, companies often have to help educate and shape those frameworks in real time — for example, helping regulators move from a weight-based to a unit-based measurement system for beverages.

faq.question: What is a common misconception people have about the cannabis industry and money?
faq.answer: Many assume cannabis operators are getting rich due to the industry's growth, but very few companies have actually turned significant profit so far, especially given regulatory costs and restrictions like federal tax code 280E.
